stories.title: Africa: U.S. Defends New HIV Funding Model As Activists Challenge PEPFAR Reforms
stories.summary: Defends New HIV Funding Model As Activists Challenge PEPFAR Reforms Felipe Varanda/IAS Activists protest during a U.S. government session on the America First Global Health Strategy at the AIDS 2026 conference in Rio de Janeiro, where officials defended new bilateral HIV funding agreements. 27 July 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — HIV activists confronted U.S. officials before the official start of the AIDS 2026 conference over sweeping changes to Washington's global HIV strategy, accusing the Trump administration of creating a public health emergency through funding cuts, while the United States defended a new financing model that it says will build more sustainable, country-led HIV programmes. At the centre of the debate is the America First Global Health Strategy , under which the United States is replacing traditional donor-funded programmes with five-year bilateral Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) that require partner countries to gradually assume greater responsibility for financing and managing their HIV responses. So far, 34 countries have signed agreements committing to increase domestic health spending between 2026 and 2030 as U.S. support is gradually reduced. Opening the pre-conference session in Rio de Janeiro on implementing the agreements, Dr Chris Akolo, Senior Technical Director for HIV at FHI 360, said the MOUs had become a central mechanism for sustaining HIV programmes and required close collaboration between governments, local implementing partners and U.S. agencies. The session brought together representatives from partner country ministries of health, local implementing organisations and U.S. government officials to discuss country ownership, governance, domestic financing and maintaining HIV service delivery during the transition.

stories.title: Sudan civil war: Civilians used as 'human shields'
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5Hedr Hundreds of thousands of Sudanese have been displaced Image: AFP Advertisement Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of El Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet. Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan. The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, project manager for the UK children's rights organization Plan International, and a native of El Obeid. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand internally displaced persons (IDP) — is under siege, he added. There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long queues of IDPs at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days." He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school. "One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because always they are in fear of something happening again," he said, adding that Plan International tried "to provide psychosocial support" for people scared of drones that could hit a classroom at any time.

stories.summary: Image source, Artists Equity Image caption, Empereur is one af the prison's most successful artists - the music video for his song Sa Ngando has been viewed 24,000 times on YouTube By Wedaeli Chibelushi Â and Â Tom Brook ,Â Talking Movies Published 26 July 2026 New Bell - a notorious prison in Douala, Cameroon - is a city within a city. The facility has its own "taxis" (inmates who whizz through congested courtyards on foot to hand deliver messages), its own law enforcement (burly prisoners who help stretched guards police the facility) and market (a string of stalls where convicts sell and buy goodies, like fried cassava and beignet pastries). Despite critics bemoaning the addition of a Superbowl-style show , external to the beautiful game's biggest event, the children's performance alongside global stars Burna Boy and Shakira was viewed by many millions around the world. Speaking to the BBC's Newsday programme , members of the dance troupe and their manager say that rising from humble beginnings in Uganda's capital, Kampala, then finding fame while balancing it all with schoolwork has taken perseverance. "Never give up... pray to God. Listen to your parents, education is first, that's all," says Sierra. She and 11-year-old Josephine are still on a high, after their World Cup appearance midway through the game that saw Spain beat Argentina at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. "I saw Messi and Lamine Yamal!" says Josephine about the two team's stars - Argentinian captain Lionel Messi and Spain's teenage winger Yamal. "I was so happy to see Messi and people watching us.

stories.summary: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Ramaphosa has been haunted by the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm in 2020 By Khanyisile Ngcobo Reporting from Johannesburg Published 24 July 2026 A South African court has ruled in favour of President Cyril Ramaphosa's bid to temporarily halt a parliamentary inquiry looking into whether he should be impeached over what has been dubbed the "Farmgate" scandal. In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa might have a case to answer after burglars stole huge sums of cash, hidden in a sofa, from his private farm. The president denied any wrongdoing. At the time MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry, but in May the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report. Ramaphosa is now challenging the findings of the panel in a separate court case to be heard in September.

"Une décision qui m'honore", a réagi Macky Sall, exprimant sa "gratitude" à son successeur. • Le président gabonais Brice Oligui Nguema a entamé, lundi, une visite d'État de trois jours en France , reçu par son homologue Emmanuel Macron pour discuter notamment de la transformation locale du manganèse - dont le Gabon est l'un des principaux producteurs - et de l'avenir du camp De Gaulle, la base militaire française à Libreville. • Les chefs d'État de la Cédéao ont signé, dimanche, à Freetown un accord intergouvernemental approuvant la construction d'un gazoduc (NMGP) devant relier le Nigeria au Maroc, lors d'un sommet ordinaire de l'institution régionale à Freetown. stories.title: Even camels can't cope: Africa's ships of the desert hit by rising temperatures
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Livestock herders in the Horn of Africa and North Africa have switched to camels over the years because of their famed resilience By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent Published 23 July 2026 Camels are famously known as the ships of the desert, but even these hardy animals are not being spared from the extremes of rising temperatures in Africa. The Afar region of north-eastern Ethiopia is one of the hottest and driest places on Earth, where nomads often lead camel caravans carrying salt through the desert. "I can see my camels suffering from extreme heat," Ali Umer, a camel herder from Semera in Afar, told the BBC. "They get blisters on their feet, their eyes become watery and the hot sand burns their skin and eats up their hair when they are sitting," said the 40-year-old who owns around 500 camels. "Within the past one month I have lost eight camel calves because of the extreme heat, it has become much more intense and difficult. "Even the wind, which used to bring cool air, now carries heat," he said, adding he had noticed these drastic changes in the temperature in recent years. He is not alone in his observations: scientists, animal welfare workers and various studies all mention stress, fatigue, dehydration, disease prevalence as direct impacts of extreme heat. The higher temperatures also indirectly make camels suffer by causing severe loss of water, vegetation, and reduced shaded areas. Image source, Corbis via Getty Images Image caption, Camels carry bricks of salt cut from the mineral-laden lakes in the Danakil Depression, where temperatures can top 50C North Africa and the Horn of Africa host around 80% of the world's largest population of dromedary camels - those with one hump.

stories.title: How Russia is luring foreign nationals to fight in Ukraine
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5HaeX Three foreign nationals recruited by Russia for its war in Ukraine Image: DW Advertisement Charles Mutoka, a 72-year-old Kenyan is in mourning for his son, Oscar Khagola Mutoka, a former soldier who traveled to Russia in the summer of 2025 to look for work. His father said that he had tried in vain to talk him out of it. Oscar did not tell him and the rest of his family exactly where he was going, but a week after leaving, he sent a picture of himself in uniform and never got back in touch again. stories.title: Why WhatsApp usernames could upset Somalia's anti-terror fight
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Somalia has an economy that heavily relies on mobile money transactions By Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Priyanka Sippy ,Â Focus on Africa podcast Published 22 July 2026 Somalia's government has told the BBC it is concerned about WhatsApp's plan to launch a new feature that would let people chat using usernames rather than phone numbers, saying it could pose a security risk. Communications and Technology Minister Ahmed Osman Dirie said it could make it harder to trace and counter criminals in a country that is still battling Islamist militants. The rollout to three billion global users of WhatsApp worldwide is expected in the coming months, allowing people to remove or change their usernames at any time. Somalia has been hit by a brutal and deadly insurgency - led by al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda affiliate - for more than two decades. In response to Somalia's concerns, WhatsApp told the BBC that the feature was not yet live, and users would still need a phone number to use the app.

Photograph: Jasmin Merdan/Alamy View image in fullscreen In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean. Photograph: Jasmin Merdan/Alamy Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy as report shows 2.69bn people can’t afford to eat well One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability. There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned. Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024.

stories.title: DR Congo neighbors boost preparedness as Ebola cases surge
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5HQAy Uganda has bolstered its preparedness after confirming at least 20 cases of Ebola Image: Hajarah Nalwadda/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Countries bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo have stepped up screening at border crossings, trained front-line health workers and activated emergency plans to reduce the risk of imported cases as the DRC battles a growing Ebola outbreak. On Monday, the DRC's Health Ministry reported that at least 930 people have died due to the illness. The DRC has recorded 2,344 cases of Bundibugyo, the virus behind the current outbreak, which the government declared on May 15. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently warned that the number of cases could be up to four times higher than what is known . In Zambia , authorities have stepped up screening at points of entry despite recording no confirmed Ebola cases.
